safety_line: Can spread dengue, Zika, and chikungunya locally. See a doctor if you develop fever, rash, or joint pain after being bitten.
traits: Bites in daytime, especially ankles and elbows
Black with white scales forming a lyre (violin) shape on top of the thorax
White banding on the legs
Breeds in bottle-cap amounts of standing water around the home

copy.what_it_means: It doesn't need a pond — a plant saucer after one afternoon storm can raise a generation in about a week. Day-biting around the patio suggests container breeding somewhere within a few hundred feet; tipping out standing water is the first, highest-value step, and a technician can evaluate what else is needed.
copy.fact: It doesn't need a pond — a plant saucer after one afternoon storm raises a generation in about a week.
copy.blurb: Southwest Florida mosquitoes breed in as little as a bottle-cap of standing water. Tipping out standing water around the property is the first, highest-value step; a technician can evaluate the rest.

tech_notes: Barrier/larvicide program per protocol. Walk property for container breeding, bromeliads, drains, plant saucers.

safety_line: Capable of spreading dengue, chikungunya, and other viruses. See a doctor if you develop fever, rash, or joint pain after being bitten.
traits: A single bold white stripe down the center of the back
Black legs with white banding on each segment
Aggressive daytime biter, peaking early morning and late afternoon
Same container-breeding habit as the yellow fever mosquito

copy.what_it_means: This species arrived in the US in used tire shipments in the 1980s and is now established statewide. Same starting point as its cousin: eliminate standing water around the home first; a technician can then treat resting areas for the adults that remain.
copy.fact: It arrived in the US in the 1980s in shipments of used tires — one of the world’s most-traveled mosquitoes.
copy.blurb: Same starting point: eliminate standing water, then a technician can treat resting areas.

tech_notes: Barrier program per protocol. Walk property for tires, containers, bromeliads, tarps holding water.

traits: Medium, plain light-brown mosquito with faint pale bands on the legs and abdomen
Bites mainly at dusk, night and dawn rather than in bright daylight
Breeds in stagnant, often dirty water: clogged gutters, ditches, birdbaths, storm drains
Rests with its body nearly parallel to the surface it lands on

look_alikes.difference: Southern house mosquito is plain brown and bites at night; Asian tiger mosquito has bold black-and-white stripes and bites during the day

safety_line: Can spread West Nile virus and other diseases carried between birds and people. See a doctor if a bite site becomes very swollen or you develop a fever after being bitten.

copy.what_it_means: Florida's most common night-biting mosquito, and the main local carrier of West Nile virus, breeding in stagnant water around the yard. Dumping standing water and routine mosquito treatment both help knock down numbers.
copy.fact: It picks up West Nile virus by feeding on infected birds, then can pass it along the next time it bites a person or another animal.

tech_notes: Primary WNV/SLE vector in FL; inspect for stagnant/organic-rich water sources (clogged gutters, drains, containers). Larvicide breeding sites and barrier-treat vegetation per label.

traits: Huge mosquito, up to about half an inch long, several times the size of a typical mosquito
Black-and-white patterned body and noticeably hairy, banded legs
Bites hard enough that people often feel it right away, unlike most mosquito bites
Shows up suddenly in large numbers after heavy rain or flooding, then fades over a few weeks

safety_line: The bite is unusually painful for a mosquito and can leave a larger welt than most mosquito bites.

copy.what_it_means: An oversized, hard-biting mosquito that appears in bursts after heavy rain or flooding, then dies back within a few weeks. It's more painful than dangerous; draining any standing floodwater and a technician-timed treatment after a big rain event both help knock numbers down.
copy.fact: Its eggs can sit dry in the soil for years and only hatch once flooding rain covers them, which is why it can appear seemingly out of nowhere after a big storm.

tech_notes: Floodwater breeder; not a significant human disease vector in FL. Barrier treatment after heavy rain/flood events; larvae are also predatory on other mosquito larvae so treat standing water directly when found.

traits: Dark, almost black mosquito with narrow white bands on the legs and abdomen

Appears in large swarms near coastal areas, mangroves and marshes after rain or high tides
Can travel miles from where it hatched on strong winds

safety_line: A persistent, aggressive daytime biter near coastal areas; it can also spread dog heartworm between pets.

copy.what_it_means: A relentless daytime-biting mosquito that breeds in mangroves and salt marshes and can swarm inland on the wind, especially near the coast after rain or high tides. Routine yard mosquito treatment and screening outdoor gathering areas both help.
copy.fact: It can fly many miles from the salt marsh where it hatched, which is why coastal neighborhoods can get swarmed even with no obvious breeding water nearby.

tech_notes: Not a primary human-disease vector locally but is a natural vector of dog heartworm and can carry other pathogens; recommend heartworm prevention discussion for pet-owning clients in heavy-pressure areas. Barrier treat vegetation; source is often off-property (marsh/mangrove) so control is largely adulticide-based.

traits: Small, worm-like creatures with a large head and a slender, curved body, floating just under the water surface
Wiggle in a quick, jerky S-shaped motion when the water is disturbed
Found in standing water: buckets, clogged gutters, plant saucers, old tires, birdbaths
Come to the surface to breathe through a short tube, then dive back down

copy.what_it_means: Wigglers in standing water are next week's biting mosquitoes. Dumping or draining the water is the fastest fix; ongoing yard treatment helps for water sources that cannot be removed, like ponds or low spots that hold rain.
copy.fact: A mosquito can go from egg to biting adult in as little as a week during warm Florida weather, which is why standing water gets refilled with mosquitoes so fast.

tech_notes: Identify and eliminate or larvicide standing water sources; note sources that cannot be drained (ornamental ponds, low-lying yard areas) for follow-up larvicide treatment per label.
